newsitem.title: UK: Back off from closer Europe, Britain's Rifkind says.
newsitem.headline: Back off from closer Europe, Britain's Rifkind says.

text.p: Two senior British ministers appealed on Monday for a slowing-down of the movement towards closer integration in the European Union.
In a speech in Stockholm, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said: "I do not believe this pace of change can be sustained."

Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke, predicting that the January 1, 1999 date for the launch of a single European currency could soon be put back, urged EU states committed to the idea to temper their enthusiasm with common sense.

Europe should not be rolling inexorably towards federal-type unity but should instead be broadening its horizons and easing members into cooperation, Rifkind told the Swedish Institute of International Affairs.

Making the first in a series of speeches in European capitals to explain Britain's view of Europe, he said too many changes were being made too fast -- from the 1986 Single European Act to the 1992 Maastricht Treaty on closer integration.

Britain's ruling Conservatives are desperately trying to present a united front ahead of a looming general election despite bitter splits between pro-Europeans and Eurosceptics. Rifkind tried to present a common ground for the two factions.

"Britain's vision for Europe is not one of rolling integration toward a single federal destiny. It is about finding the right balance between supernationalism and inter-governmentalism; using supernationalism where it is necessary, but only where it is necessary," he said.

"Our vision of the EU 10 years from now is of a Union enlarged to represent almost all of Europe, not just its wealthy western half," he added. What he called "supranational integration" was good in some areas, Rifkind conceded.
"We need it to sustain the single market, the competition and state aid regimes, the common agricultural and fisheries policies."
Cooperation also made sense in fighting drug trafficking, for example, or on visa policies, Rifkind said.
"But these areas are different from the Single Market or the Common Agricultural Policy," he added.

"They go to the heart of the relationship between the citizen and the state. It may be that in some countries people are ready to have a European Police Force patrolling their streets, to be subject to arrest and detention by European justice authorities...But in Britain they are not."
Clarke, speaking from Davos, Switzerland to BBC radio, recognised there was a strong political will across much of continental Europe to go ahead with a single currency.

"But in my view that should be combined with common sense," he said. "Nobody should contemplate EMU (economic and monetary union) unless countries are genuinely convergent and are going to stay convergent in the economic conditions."
Clarke said it was unlikely that enough EU states would have convergent economies in time for the new currency to be launched on the planned date.
"Personally I think there will be a postponement of it. Perhaps in a few months, perhaps a little after that," he said.
